title: Pan Am 759

location.name: Kenner, Louisiana (residential area near New Orleans International Airport)

summary: Pan American World Airways Flight 759, a Boeing 727-235 carrying 145 persons (7 crew, 137 passengers, 1 nonrevenue jumpseat passenger), crashed in the residential area of Kenner, Louisiana, immediately after takeoff from runway 10 at New Orleans International Airport on July 9, 1982. The aircraft lifted off, climbed to 95-150 feet above ground level, then began to descend, striking trees and residential structures. Eight persons on the ground were also killed. The aircraft encountered microburst-induced wind shear producing a strong downdraft and decreasing headwind during the critical liftoff and initial climb phase.
probable_cause: The aircraft's encounter with microburst-induced wind shear during liftoff, which imposed a downdraft and a decreasing headwind. Contributing factors included the limited capability of then-current wind shear detection technology, the limited capability of the aircraft to climb out of wind shear with heavy loading, and inadequate wind shear training and recognition by the flightcrew. (p. 72)

factors.evidence: The aircraft's encounter with microburst-induced wind shear during the liftoff imposed a downdraft and a decreasing headwind, which prevented the aircraft from continuing to climb. The microburst produced strong downdraft with wind direction changes from 040 at 8 knots to 070 at 17 knots with peak gusts to 23 knots in approximately 3 minutes. (p. 64-82)

At the time of Flight 759's takeoff, there were showers over the east end of the airport and to the east of the airport along the airplane's intended takeoff path. The winds were gusty, variable, and swirling. Low level wind shear alerts were in effect all quadrants with a frontal system passing overhead. (p. 8)

The flightcrew would have had difficulty recognizing and reacting to the wind shear in time for the aircraft's descent to be stopped. At the time of the accident, wind shear recognition training was limited and Low Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWSAS) technology was not widely available in commercial aviation. (p. 68-70)

The aircraft struck a line of trees at an altitude of about 50 feet and crashed into the residential area of Kenner at coordinates 29 degrees 59 min 15 sec N, 90 degrees 14 min 08 sec W, destroying six houses and substantially damaging five others. One hundred thirty-seven passengers, 7 crew members, and 8 persons on the ground were killed. (p. 9-10)

events.text: Flight 759 (Clipper 759) taxied from its gate at New Orleans International Airport with 7 crewmembers, 1 nonrevenue passenger on cockpit jumpseat, and 137 passengers (145 total) aboard. Takeoff gross weight 170,000 lbs.

Ground control advised another aircraft of low level wind shear alerts in northeast quadrants of the airport with relevant wind directions and speeds. Clipper 759's radio received this advisory while taxiing.

First officer requested wind check. Ground control replied: Wind now 070 degrees at 17, peak gusts 23, and we have low level wind shear alerts all quadrants, appears to be a frontal passing overhead right now, we're right in the middle of everything.
Captain advised first officer to let your airspeed build up on takeoff and said they would turn off the air conditioning packs for the takeoff to enable increase of EPRs on engines 1 and 3 to 1.92.
Clipper 759 informed tower that it was ready for takeoff from runway 10. Takeoff briefing completed; target EPR 1.90 engines 1 and 3, 1.92 engine 2; V1=138 KIAS, Vr=138 KIAS, V2=151 KIAS.
Local controller cleared Flight 759 for takeoff; first officer acknowledged. This was the last radio transmission received from Clipper 759.

Local controller cleared Eastern Flight 956 to land runway 10 and advised: Wind 070 at 17, heavy Boeing just landed said a ten knot wind shear at about a hundred feet on the final. This advisory was also received on Clipper 759's radio.
Clipper 759 began its takeoff from runway 10. CVR showed Vr and V2 callouts made by captain. Aircraft was at approximately 7,000 feet down the runway at liftoff point.
Aircraft lifted off runway 10, climbed in wings-level attitude to altitude of 95-150 feet above ground level in normal takeoff manner according to witnesses. Aircraft then began to descend.

Aircraft in descent approximately 2,376 feet from end of runway 10, struck line of trees at altitude of about 50 feet above ground level while still in noseup attitude (7-10 degrees by witness reports), indicating aircraft was in stall or low-speed condition.

Aircraft crashed into residential area of Kenner, Louisiana (coordinates 29 degrees 59 min 15 sec N, 90 degrees 14 min 08 sec W), destroying six houses and substantially damaging five others. Aircraft was destroyed in impact, explosion, and subsequent fire. Total 153 fatal injuries (137 passengers, 7 crew, 1 fetus, 8 on ground); 1 serious injury on ground.

recommendations.text: Expedite the installation of Low Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWSAS) equipment at all major commercial airports, with particular emphasis on those in areas prone to thunderstorm activity and microbursts.

Develop and require specific training for airline crews on recognition and avoidance of low-altitude wind shear, including tactical maneuvers to escape wind shear encounters during takeoff and landing phases.
Evaluate and develop methods to improve aircraft performance during wind shear encounters, particularly regarding climb capability, engine response, and automation logic to assist flight crews.

Require installation of airborne wind shear detection systems on commercial transport category aircraft, to provide real-time wind shear awareness to flight crews during takeoff and landing operations.

safety_changes: Development and installation of Low Level Wind Shear Alert System (LLWSAS) at major airports
Implementation of airborne wind shear detection systems on commercial aircraft
Enhanced wind shear recognition training for airline flight crews
Improved microburst forecasting and nowcasting capabilities
Better communication of wind shear information between ATC and flight crews
